title: What Python Project Should I Build Next? What Job Postings Suggest
text:
When I started learning Python as a college freshman, deciding what to build next was not obvious. Backend development, databases, and machine learning all seemed useful, but I wanted a project with a clear purpose.
By “build,” I mean completing a small, working Python project that I could include in a portfolio to show what I can do. An application tracker or a simple machine learning classifier would be examples. I wanted to use job postings to help narrow that choice, and I thought the same exercise could be useful to other learners deciding how to put their Python knowledge into practice.
So my question is: what do the topic tags on Python job postings suggest about whether a beginner should start with a backend application or a machine learning project?
But only looking at job postings online cannot tell me which project will get someone hired. They can give me a limited view of the work employers advertise and help me make a more informed learning choice.

title: What Python Project Should I Build Next? What Job Postings Suggest
text:
Collecting the data
So I decide to use the public Python.org Job Board and collect only its first listing page. Each row represents one listing URL. I will extract the title, location, topic tags, posting dates, and links.
I use R to read the webpage, identify the repeated job cards, and extract the same fields from each card. A selector tells R where to find information such as a job title or its topic tags. This turns the listings into a table that I can compare systematically.
For ethical collection as required, the code does not bypass logins, CAPTCHAs, paywalls, or other access restrictions. If the website denies access, I would stop collecting.


Code
url <- "https://www.python.org/jobs/"
html_file <- file.path(data_dir, "python_jobs.html")
metadata_file <- file.path(data_dir, "collection_metadata.csv")

# Set it FALSE will reuse the snapshot. If none exists, collect one page.
# I will set it TRUE only if when I want to deliberately collecting a new snapshot.
refresh <- FALSE
new_snapshot <- refresh || !file.exists(html_file)

if (new_snapshot) {
  page <- read_html(url)
} else {
  page <- read_html(html_file)
}

job_cards <- page |> html_elements("ol.list-recent-jobs > li")

if (length(job_cards) == 0) {
  stop("No job cards found. Check the page before continuing.")
}

jobs_raw <- tibble(
  title = job_cards |>
    html_element(".listing-company-name a") |> html_text2(),
  location = job_cards |>
    html_element(".listing-location") |> html_text2(),
  tags = job_cards |>
    html_element(".listing-job-type") |> html_text2(),
  posted_date = job_cards |>
    html_element("time") |> html_attr("datetime"),
  job_url = job_cards |>
    html_element(".listing-company-name a") |> html_attr("href")
)

jobs_raw <- jobs_raw |>
  mutate(job_url = xml2::url_absolute(job_url, url))

if (any(is.na(jobs_raw$title) | str_squish(jobs_raw$title) == "") ||
    any(is.na(jobs_raw$job_url) | jobs_raw$job_url == "")) {
  stop("A title or link is missing. Check the extraction before continuing.")
}

if (new_snapshot) {
  metadata <- tibble(
    source_url = url,
    snapshot_date_utc = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d", tz = "UTC"),
    retrieval_method = "Downloaded with rvest::read_html(url)",
    scope = "First listing page only"
  )
  xml2::write_html(page, html_file)
  write_csv(metadata, metadata_file)
} else {
  metadata <- read_csv(metadata_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
}

snapshot_date <- metadata$snapshot_date_utc[1]

# Display the first five collected listings.
knitr::kable(
  jobs_raw |> select(title, location, posted_date) |> head(5),
  col.names = c("Job title", "Location", "Posting date"),
  caption = "First five collected listings"
)

title: What Python Project Should I Build Next? What Job Postings Suggest
text:
Cleaning the information
Now I want to remove all extra spaces, convert the posting dates, and remove duplicate URLs. I also record which listings have no topic tags. Missing tags are missing information, so they do not show that a job requires none of these skills.
I mainly focus on six broad labels: Back end, Machine Learning, Database, Front end, Cloud, and Web. I selected these labels to compare backend and machine learning with related areas that could become part of a Python project. They are not an exhaustive list of employers’ requirements. str_detect() checks whether each label appears, and sum() later counts the TRUE values.


Code
jobs <- jobs_raw |>
  mutate(
    title = str_squish(title),
    location = str_squish(location),
    tags = coalesce(str_squish(tags), ""),
    tags_missing = tags == "",
    posted_date = as.Date(substr(posted_date, 1, 10))
  ) |>
  distinct(job_url, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    backend = str_detect(tags, fixed("Back end", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    machine_learning = str_detect(tags, fixed("Machine Learning", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    database = str_detect(tags, fixed("Database", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    frontend = str_detect(tags, fixed("Front end", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    cloud = str_detect(tags, fixed("Cloud", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    web = str_detect(tags, fixed("Web", ignore_case = TRUE))
  )

#save the cleaned data
write.csv(
  jobs,
  here("blog", "posts", "post2", "data", "jobs_clean.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

#read the saved data for the analysis
jobs <- read.csv(
  here("blog", "posts", "post2", "data", "jobs_clean.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

#convert posting dates back to dates after reading the CSV
jobs$posted_date <- as.Date(jobs$posted_date)

n_total <- nrow(jobs)
n_duplicates <- nrow(jobs_raw) - n_total
n_missing <- sum(jobs$tags_missing)
n_missing_dates <- sum(is.na(jobs$posted_date))
n_missing_locations <- sum(is.na(jobs$location) | jobs$location == "")
n_backend <- sum(jobs$backend)
n_ml <- sum(jobs$machine_learning)
n_both <- sum(jobs$backend & jobs$machine_learning)

#display the cleaning checks.
quality <- tibble(
  Check = c(
    "Job cards extracted",
    "Unique listing URLs",
    "Duplicate URLs removed",
    "Listings without topic tags",
    "Listings with missing dates",
    "Listings with missing locations"
  ),
  Count = c(
    nrow(jobs_raw),
    n_total,
    n_duplicates,
    n_missing,
    n_missing_dates,
    n_missing_locations

)

write.csv(

title: What Python Project Should I Build Next? What Job Postings Suggest
section: Do backend and machine learning appear together?
text:
Do backend and machine learning appear together?
The ranking tells me which tags are common, but I also want to know whether backend and machine learning appear on the same listings. That matters for the project choice: if employers advertise the two together, I have a reason to explore a project that connects them, such as a classifier inside an application. I use case_when() to put each posting into exactly one group and make that overlap easier to see.


Code
overlap <- jobs |>
  mutate(
    group = case_when(
      tags_missing ~ "No tags shown",
      backend & machine_learning ~ "Both backend and ML",
      backend ~ "Backend tag; no ML tag",
      machine_learning ~ "ML tag; no backend tag",
      TRUE ~ "Neither selected tag"
    )
  ) |>
  count(group, name = "postings", sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(percent = round(100 * postings / n_total, 1))

write.csv(
  overlap,
  here("blog", "posts", "post2", "results", "tables", "topic_overlap.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

title: What Python Project Should I Build Next? What Job Postings Suggest
text:
What I would build next
For my next general Python project, I would start with a small backend application. Backend appears at least as often as ML in this sample, so it is a reasonable area to prioritize when choosing between the two.
I would build an application tracker that lets a user add a job application, update its status, and retrieve saved records. Next, I would connect it to a small database and check how it handles missing or invalid inputs.
The overlap also gives me a reason to connect the two areas. For a project that combines both, I could connect the job description classifier to the application tracker and show its prediction through the application. That would let me practice using a model inside a working application.
This is my proposed learning sequence. The listings do not specifically request an application tracker, a particular database, or one framework. The practical decision is about what to build next, not a claim that one project guarantees employment.

title: What Python Project Should I Build Next? What Job Postings Suggest
text:
Limits of the analysis
This is a small, international sample from the first page of one job board and it is not a random sample of Python jobs. So the employers may appear more than once, and different URLs do not necessarily represent different vacancies.
The tags are broad descriptions rather than a complete reading of each job’s requirements as I did not measure experience requirements, salaries, applicant competition, or hiring outcomes. So, I cannot conclude that the postings are entry level jobs or that learning a frequent topic causes a higher chance of receiving an offer.
For someone choosing a Python portfolio project, my recommendation from this snapshot is to start with a small application tracker. A user should be able to save an application, update its status, and retrieve it later. I would get that basic workflow working and write clear instructions for running it before adding a job-description classifier. The overlap between the tags makes that extension worth exploring. If you are making a similar choice, use this as a starting point, then read full descriptions of jobs that interest you to decide which features are worth practicing.
My goal here is to help someone who knows basic Python choose a manageable project for a portfolio. If you are unsure what to make next, the approach is simple: use job tags to narrow your options, read a few full descriptions, and choose one useful task to practice. That gives you a specific next step and something concrete to show others, while leaving room for your own interests and current skills.

title: Education and Unemployment Through the Pandemic and Recovery
text:
The unemployment rate gives us a quick picture of the job market, but people with different levels of education may have very different experiences. I wanted to look more closely at those differences. How did unemployment vary by education from 2019 to 2024, and does the latest comparison also hold within age groups? I start with 2019 to see where each group stood before the pandemic. Then I look at the change in 2020 and the pattern through 2024. Finally, I compare education groups among people of similar ages. This helps separate a group’s starting unemployment rate from how much its situation changed. ## Data and approach For this post, I use IPUMS CPS Basic Monthly data covering all 72 months from January 2019 through December 2024. I focus on civilians ages 25–64 who are in the labor force. Starting at 25 reduces the influence of people still finishing their initial education, while stopping at 64 limits differences related to retirement. I use four education groups: less than high school, high school or equivalent, some college or an associate’s degree, and a bachelor’s degree or more. The unemployment rate measures unemployed people, including those on temporary layoff, as a share of the labor force. People outside the labor force are left out of that calculation.


Show the R code
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

post_dir <- here("blog", "posts", "post3")

data_file <- file.path(
  post_dir, "data", "cps_2019_2024.csv.gz"
)

results_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "results")

dir.create(
  results_dir,
  showWarnings = FALSE,
  recursive = TRUE
)

stopifnot(file.exists(data_file))

cps_raw <- read_csv(
  data_file,
  col_select = c(YEAR, MONTH, ASECFLAG, AGE, EDUC, EMPSTAT, WTFINL),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_double()),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

stopifnot(nrow(problems(cps_raw)) == 0)
stopifnot(sum(cps_raw$ASECFLAG == 1, na.rm = TRUE) == 0)
#want to check every requested year and month is present.
cps_raw <- cps_raw |> filter(YEAR %in% 2019:2024)
month_check <- cps_raw |> distinct(YEAR, MONTH)
stopifnot(
  nrow(month_check) == 72,
  all(month_check$MONTH %in% 1:12)
)
education_order <- c(
  "Less than high school", "High school",
  "Some college / associate", "Bachelor's or more"
)
# keep those employed and unemployed adults
cps_eligible <- cps_raw |>
  filter(AGE >= 25, AGE <= 64, EMPSTAT %in% c(10, 12, 20, 21, 22))

cps <- cps_eligible |>
  mutate(
    education = case_when(
      EDUC >= 2 & EDUC <= 71 ~ "Less than high school",
      EDUC == 73 ~ "High school",
      EDUC %in% c(81, 91, 92) ~ "Some college / associate",
      EDUC %in% c(111, 123, 124, 125) ~ "Bachelor's or more",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    education = factor(education, levels = education_order),
    unemployed = EMPSTAT %in% c(20, 21, 22),
    age_group = case_when(
      AGE <= 34 ~ "25–34",
      AGE <= 44 ~ "35–44",
      AGE <= 54 ~ "45–54",
      TRUE ~ "55–64"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(education), !is.na(WTFINL), is.finite(WTFINL), WTFINL > 0)
excluded_n <- nrow(cps_eligible) - nrow(cps)
#the formula for annual unemployment rate is: 100 x weighted unemployed / weighted labor force.
#Pooling all 12 months makes this a ratio of annual-average population totals.
annual <- cps |>
  group_by(YEAR, education) |>
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    months = n_distinct(MONTH),
    unemployment_rate = 100 * sum(WTFINL * unemployed) / sum(WTFINL),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
#we require all four education groups in each year, with all 12 months.
stopifnot(
  nrow(annual) == 24,
  all(annual$months == 12),
  all(annual$unemployment_rate >= 0 & annual$unemployment_rate <= 100)
)
#Figure 2: use pivot_wider() to put 2019 and 2020 on the same row.
shock <- annual |>
  filter(YEAR %in% c(2019, 2020)) |>
  select(education, YEAR, unemployment_rate) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = YEAR, values_from = unemployment_rate, names_prefix = "rate_"
  ) |>
  mutate(change_pp = rate_2020 - rate_2019)
#Figure 3: calculate the same weighted rate within four age groups in 2024.
by_age <- cps |>
  filter(YEAR == 2024) |>
  group_by(YEAR, age_group, education) |>
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    months = n_distinct(MONTH),
    unemployment_rate = 100 * sum(WTFINL * unemployed) / sum(WTFINL),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
stopifnot(nrow(by_age) == 16, all(by_age$months == 12))
#stacks the three summary tables.
all_results <- bind_rows(
  annual |> mutate(result = "annual_rates"),
  shock |> mutate(result = "change_2019_2020"),
  by_age |> mutate(result = "age_rates_2024")
)
write_csv(all_results, file.path(results_dir, "summary_results.csv"))
#make the displayed numbers easier to read.
comparison <- annual |>
  select(YEAR, education, unemployment_rate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = education, values_from = unemployment_rate)
baseline <- comparison |> filter(YEAR == 2019)
latest <- comparison |> filter(YEAR == 2024)
hs_change <- shock$change_pp[shock$education == "High school"]
college_change <- shock$change_pp[shock$education == "Bachelor's or more"]
age_comparison <- by_age |>
  select(age_group, education, unemployment_rate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = education, values_from = unemployment_rate)
age_count <- sum(age_comparison$`High school` > age_comparison$`Bachelor's or more`)
change_description <- if_else(
  hs_change > college_change,
  "The high school group saw the larger change in its unemployment rate.",
  "The high school group's change was no larger than the college group's."
)
takeaway <- if_else(
  latest$`High school` > latest$`Bachelor's or more`,
  "In 2024, unemployment was lower among people with at least a bachelor's degree than among those whose highest qualification was high school.",
  "In 2024, having at least a bachelor's degree was not associated with a lower unemployment rate than having only a high school diploma."
)
#use the same source note and figure dimensions throughout the post.
source_note <- "Source: IPUMS CPS, University of Minnesota. Weighted using WTFINL."
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.5, dpi = 150)


After cleaning, I have 2,992,422 person-month records. I leave out 0 otherwise eligible records because their education or weight cannot be used. The CPS interviews some people in several months, so the record count includes repeat interviews. Each respondent represents a different number of people. To account for that, I use the WTFINL weight recommended by IPUMS. For each group and year, I add up the weighted unemployed and divide by the weighted labor force, then multiply by 100. Pooling all 12 months gives the ratio of annual-average totals. I do not apply seasonal adjustment. ## 1. How did the education groups move over time?


Show the R code
figure1 <- ggplot(
  annual,
  aes(x = YEAR, y = unemployment_rate)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ education, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2019:2024) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Unemployment by education, 2019–2024",
    subtitle = "Civilian labor-force participants ages 25–64; identical axes",
    x = NULL, y = "Annual unemployment rate (%)",
    caption = source_note
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
figure1





Show the R code
ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "figure1_trend.png"), figure1,
       width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 300)


I first look at the full six-year picture. In 2019, unemployment was 3.8% among people with only a high school diploma, compared with 2.1% among those with at least a bachelor’s degree. In 2024, those rates were 4.4% and 2.3%. Each panel uses the same scale, so we can compare both the levels and the paths over time. The next figure looks directly at how much each group changed in 2020. ## 2. How large was the change in 2020?


Show the R code
figure2 <- ggplot(shock, aes(x = change_pp, y = education)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "The change in unemployment from 2019 to 2020",
    subtitle = "Annual rate in 2020 minus annual rate in 2019; ages 25–64",
    x = "Change in percentage points", y = NULL,
    caption = source_note
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
figure2





Show the R code
ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "figure2_change.png"), figure2,
       width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 300)


To make the 2020 change easier to compare, I subtract each group’s 2019 rate from its 2020 rate. The change was 5.3 percentage points for the high school group and 2.7 points for the bachelor’s-or-more group. The high school group saw the larger change in its unemployment rate. For context, going from 4% to 7% would be a three-percentage-point increase. These changes describe the groups’ unemployment rates; they do not track which individual workers lost jobs. ## 3. Does the latest comparison hold within age groups?


Show the R code
figure3 <- ggplot(by_age, aes(x = unemployment_rate, y = education)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ age_group, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Unemployment by education within age groups",
    subtitle = "2024 annual rates; civilian labor-force participants; identical axes",
    x = "Unemployment rate (%)", y = NULL,
    caption = source_note
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
figure3





Show the R code
ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "figure3_age.png"), figure3,
       width = 9, height = 7, dpi = 300)


I also wanted to check whether the overall comparison holds among people of similar ages. In 2024, the high school group had higher unemployment than the bachelor’s-or-more group in 4 of the four age groups. Breaking the results down this way shows where the overall pattern holds and where it does not. People within an age group can still have different backgrounds and jobs, so this does not remove every possible explanation for the gap.
What stands out to me is how much the high-school–bachelor’s gap differs by age. Among adults ages 25–34, unemployment was 6.0% for the high school group and 2.9% for the bachelor’s-or-more group, a gap of 3.1 percentage points. Among those ages 55–64, the rates were 2.8% and 2.4%, leaving a gap of only 0.4 points. This helps explain why the age breakdown matters: the overall comparison holds among people of similar ages, but the difference between these two education groups is much wider among younger adults. ## How I read these results I would be careful about saying education alone caused these differences. People with different qualifications also work in different occupations, industries, and places. The analysis leaves out people outside the labor force, and IPUMS reports pandemic-era nonresponse and employment-status misclassification. I keep the reported classifications. I also do not calculate confidence intervals that account for the survey design, so I would not read too much into small gaps. My takeaway: In 2024, unemployment was lower among people with at least a bachelor’s degree than among those whose highest qualification was high school. Looking at the trend, the change in 2020, and the age groups gives a fuller picture of how unemployment differed across education levels. These comparisons help describe who was struggling in the job market, while leaving open the question of how much of the difference education itself explains.
The age results also help me be more specific about that takeaway. The high-school–bachelor’s gap appears in every age group, but it is largest at ages 25–34 and smallest at ages 55–64. I would therefore be cautious about using the overall average to describe the gap at every age. This is a comparison of different groups in 2024, so it does not show that the value of education declines as an individual gets older. Data source: IPUMS CPS, University of Minnesota. Variable definitions: EDUC, EMPSTAT, and WTFINL. All analysis code appears in this post; the repository README provides replication instructions.

title: Did Paychecks Keep Up With Prices?
text:
In 2022 it felt like everyone I knew was complaining about prices: rent, groceries, gas. But a lot of people also got big raises around then. So which one won?
My question: since COVID started, have paychecks kept up with prices, and did some industries do better than others?
The short answer: barely. The average paycheck has grown 32% since February 2020, but prices grew 29%, so an hour of work buys only about 3% more than it did before COVID.
This matters because your paycheck number isn’t what you live on. If your pay rises 10% but prices rise 15%, you can buy less than before. Economists call the paycheck number the nominal wage and what it buys the real wage, the one people actually feel.

title: Did Paychecks Keep Up With Prices?
text:
Data
My data comes from the Bureau of Labor Statistics via FRED: average hourly earnings for private-sector workers, overall and for 13 industries, plus the Consumer Price Index (CPI), all monthly and seasonally adjusted.
I compare February 2020, the last month before COVID hit, with August 2026, the newest month with both series when I downloaded the data. My code downloads each series once and saves it in data/raw/, so results stay the same every time I render.

wages = get_fred("CES0500000003").rename(columns={"value": "wage"})

title: Did Paychecks Keep Up With Prices?
text:
Limits
These are averages, so they don’t describe every worker, and they leave out benefits, hours, and taxes. The CPI is an average basket too, so your own inflation could be different. And this shows what happened, not exactly why.

title: Did Paychecks Keep Up With Prices?
text:
Takeaway
So, did paychecks keep up? Yes, but barely. Pay rose 32.3% and prices rose 28.9%, leaving a real raise of about 2.7%, less than a dollar an hour. Workers fell behind for two years during the inflation surge, slowly caught up, and lower-paid industries like restaurants and hotels did best.
The biggest lesson for me is that a raise only means something next to the inflation rate. A 5% raise in 2022 was actually a pay cut, while a 4% raise in 2024 was a real gain. That’s why so many people felt poorer in 2022 even though their paychecks were growing. And with prices edging ahead of pay again in 2026, the next few months are worth watching.

Data source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, via FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis): average hourly earnings for all private-sector employees (CES0500000003) and 13 industries (CES1000000003 to CES8000000003), and the CPI-U (CPIAUCSL), all monthly and seasonally adjusted. BLS data are public domain. Read programmatically from FRED’s CSV links on October 4, 2026 and cached in data/raw/. The wage numbers come from the BLS’s monthly survey of employers (Current Employment Statistics), and the CPI-U covers urban consumers, over 90% of the U.S. population. Code to reproduce the analysis is in the GitHub repository.

section: Adjusting for inflation: the one transformation that matters
text:
Adjusting for inflation: the one transformation that matters
A dollar in 2026 doesn’t buy what it did in 2020, so the one transformation that really matters is taking inflation out. The basic idea fits in one line:
real income growth ≈ nominal income growth - inflation
In plain words, your raise minus the rise in prices is how much better off you really are. So in my example above, a 10% raise with 15% inflation means real pay falls roughly 5%.
That shortcut is fine for one year, but over several years it overstates the gain a little (since 2020 it would give 3.4% instead of the exact 2.7%). So to compare pay across years, I turned every month’s wage into August 2026 dollars:
real wage = wage * CPI(Aug 2026) / CPI(that month)
I also calculated 12-month growth rates, which is how inflation is usually reported in the news. Figure 1 and Figure 3 use the real wage, and Figure 2 compares the two growth rates.

title: Same Region, Different Incomes
text:
In my last post, the important question was what a paycheck could buy. This time, I’m looking at where income is concentrated. We often describe whole regions as wealthy, but does that description fit every place within them?
My question: where are Pennsylvania’s higher-income counties concentrated, and how does Philadelphia compare with nearby counties?
The short answer: the southeast stands out, but Philadelphia tells a different story. Chester County’s median household income is roughly twice Philadelphia’s. That’s a substantial gap between places in the same part of the state.
That’s why I wanted to put the numbers on a map. A statewide summary gives an overall income level, but it cannot show whether neighboring counties look alike. Seeing the counties together lets me ask whether higher incomes are spread across Pennsylvania or concentrated in particular places.

title: Same Region, Different Incomes
text:
Data and method
I use the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2020–2024 American Community Survey and 2024 county boundaries, covering all 67 Pennsylvania counties. These are five-year estimates, not a measure of income growth between 2020 and 2024.
Pooling five years helps provide estimates for smaller places, but it also means this is not a snapshot of a single year.
The variable, B19013_001E, measures median household income in inflation-adjusted 2024 dollars. Imagine lining up households from lowest to highest income: the median sits in the middle. It isn’t the average paycheck. A household can include several earners, and its income can include sources beyond wages.
To make the map, I match each income estimate to the right county boundary using its Census identifier, GEOID. The code checks that all 67 counties matched and uses an equal-area projection, EPSG:5070. It also saves the downloads, cleaned data, figures, and tables, so the analysis can be repeated from the same inputs.


Code
from pathlib import Path
import os
import requests
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

raw = Path("data/raw")
processed = Path("data/processed")
figures = Path("results/figures")
tables = Path("results/tables")

for folder in [raw, processed, figures, tables]:
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

zip_file = raw / "cb_2024_us_county_500k.zip"
csv_file = raw / "acs_2024_pa_county_income.csv"

if not zip_file.exists():
    url = "https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2024/shp/cb_2024_us_county_500k.zip"
    response = requests.get(url, timeout=120)
    response.raise_for_status()
    zip_file.write_bytes(response.content)

if not csv_file.exists():
    key = os.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY")
    assert key, "Set CENSUS_API_KEY in .Renviron and restart R."

    params = {
        "get": "NAME,B19013_001E",
        "for": "county:*",
        "in": "state:42",
        "key": key
    }

    try:
        response = requests.get(
            "https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5",
            params=params,
            timeout=60
        )
    except requests.RequestException:
        raise RuntimeError("Census download failed; check your connection.") from None

    assert response.status_code == 200, "Check your activated Census key."
    data = response.json()
    pd.DataFrame(data[1:], columns=data[0]).to_csv(csv_file, index=False)

counties = gpd.read_file(zip_file)
counties = counties.loc[
    counties.STATEFP == "42", ["GEOID", "NAME", "geometry"]
]

acs = pd.read_csv(csv_file, dtype=str)
acs["GEOID"] = acs.state.str.zfill(2) + acs.county.str.zfill(3)
acs["income"] = pd.to_numeric(acs.B19013_001E, errors="coerce")

pa = counties.merge(
    acs[["GEOID", "income"]],
    on="GEOID",
    how="left",
    validate="one_to_one"
)

assert len(pa) == 67 and pa.GEOID.is_unique
assert pa.income.notna().all() and pa.income.gt(0).all()

pa = pa.to_crs("EPSG:5070")
pa[["GEOID", "NAME", "income"]].to_csv(
    processed / "county_income.csv", index=False
)

Figure 1: County median household income, 2020–2024 ACS; 2024 dollars. Source: U.S. Census Bureau.




Start with the geography in Figure 1. Each shape is one county, and darker blue means higher median household income. Chester, Bucks, and Montgomery have the three highest estimates. They sit close together in southeastern Pennsylvania, which is why that corner stands out.
Philadelphia complicates the picture. It belongs to the same region, but its much lighter shade reflects a lower median. The difference isn’t just between opposite ends of Pennsylvania. It also appears among counties within the southeast.
Lower-income counties also appear in the north, including Cameron, and parts of the southwest. So I wouldn’t read this as a simple “wealthy east, poorer west” map. There are differences within those broad areas too.
One detail matters when reading it: a large county takes up more space, but that doesn’t mean it contains more people. A wide stretch of pale-blue counties can dominate the picture even when many residents live in smaller counties. The map shows where income levels are located, not the share of Pennsylvanians living at each level.

title: Same Region, Different Incomes
section: What these figures cannot tell us
text:
What these figures cannot tell us
County medians hide differences among neighborhoods and households. Two counties could have similar medians even if income were distributed very differently within them. These figures alone cannot tell us how many households are struggling or how incomes vary between neighborhoods.
The ACS is also a survey, so these numbers have uncertainty. Bucks and Montgomery illustrate why that matters: their estimates are only $849 apart. Without examining the margins of error, I would not put much weight on which ranks second or third. I have not tested whether the differences shown are statistically significant.
And “2024 dollars” puts incomes on the same time basis; it doesn’t adjust for local living costs. The $65,255 gap is also not an estimate of what a family would gain by moving to Chester County. Jobs, housing, and household composition could matter, but these figures do not establish causes.

title: Same Region, Different Incomes
text:
Takeaway
So, where are higher incomes concentrated? Pennsylvania’s highest county estimates are in the southeast, but Philadelphia has a much lower median than the four nearby counties in this comparison.
A region’s reputation can only tell us so much. The statewide map points to a concentration of higher incomes. Looking more closely shows a substantial divide inside that same region. Before describing an area as wealthy, it helps to ask which places that description actually fits.

Data sources: U.S. Census Bureau: 2020–2024 American Community Survey five-year estimates, median household income (B19013_001E), and 2024 cartographic county boundary files at 1:500,000 scale. The analysis covers all 67 Pennsylvania counties. Income figures describe annual household income in inflation-adjusted 2024 dollars and are survey estimates. Data are downloaded programmatically from the Census API and boundary-file archive, then cached in data/raw/. Cleaned data are saved in data/processed/, with figures and comparison tables in results/. The complete analysis code is included in this post’s Quarto file, with replication instructions in README.md. Project repository: GitHub.

title: Same Region, Different Incomes
text:
What the data measure
I use the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2020–2024 American Community Survey and 2024 county boundaries, covering all 67 Pennsylvania counties. Here, Philadelphia means Philadelphia County, which covers the city.
The ACS combines survey responses collected over five years to produce estimates for places of different sizes. The income figures describe annual household income, not five years of earnings added together. They also do not measure how much income grew between 2020 and 2024.
My variable, B19013_001E, is median household income in inflation-adjusted 2024 dollars. Imagine lining up households from lowest to highest income: the median sits in the middle.
For example, suppose five households earn $30,000, $40,000, $50,000, $80,000, and $200,000. The median is $50,000. That gives us a way to describe the middle of the group without letting the highest income dominate the number.
Using a median also lets us compare differently sized counties: having more households does not automatically give a county a higher median.
Household income is also different from the paycheck measure in my last post. A household can have several earners, and income can include sources beyond wages. So this comparison describes household income levels; it does not tell us what someone would earn for doing the same job in each county.

title: Does One Year’s Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
In my last post, nearby counties had very different incomes. This time, I wanted to follow families: how closely does adult income resemble parental income, and does the answer depend on when we measure it?
Think about someone finishing graduate school at 30. Their income today may say little about where they will be at 40. That makes the timing of an income comparison worth questioning.

Sources

title: Does One Year’s Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Building the match with SQL
Python creates people, containing family links, and incomes, containing annual records. SELECT chooses columns; GROUP BY gathers each person’s years. Aggregation turns these rows into a summary: AVG calculates mean income and COUNT checks completeness. HAVING requires three observations. CASE WHEN and MAX retrieve the middle year’s value; Python supplies the years through ? placeholders.

summary_sql = """
SELECT person_id,
       AVG(income) AS mean_income,
       MAX(CASE WHEN year = ? THEN income END) AS one_income,
       MAX(CASE WHEN year = ? THEN age END) AS age,
       MAX(CASE WHEN year = ? THEN family_id END) AS home
FROM incomes
WHERE year IN (?, ?, ?)
GROUP BY person_id
HAVING COUNT(income) = 3
"""
windows = [("parents", [1984, 1985, 1986], 1985),
           ("early", [1999, 2001, 2003], 2001),
           ("later", [2009, 2011, 2013], 2011)]
for table, years, center in windows:
    summary = pd.read_sql_query(summary_sql, conn,
                                params=[center, center, center] + years)
    summary.to_sql(table, conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")
Path("sql/income_summary.sql").write_text(summary_sql)

JOIN connects these summaries using person identifiers. Each ID combines an original family number and person number, distinguishing siblings. The recorded father ID establishes parenthood; 1985 family IDs and membership numbers confirm shared residence. Summarizing first avoids counting each child repeatedly.

match_sql = """
SELECT c.person_id AS child_id, c.father_id,
       p.one_income AS parent_one, p.mean_income AS parent_mean,
       e.one_income AS early_one, e.mean_income AS early_mean,
       l.one_income AS later_one, l.mean_income AS later_mean
FROM people AS c
JOIN parents AS p ON c.father_id = p.person_id
JOIN early AS e ON c.person_id = e.person_id
JOIN later AS l ON c.person_id = l.person_id
WHERE e.age BETWEEN 27 AND 32
  AND p.age BETWEEN 30 AND 60
  AND c.home_1985 = p.home
  AND c.sequence_1985 BETWEEN 1 AND 20
ORDER BY child_id
"""
matched = pd.read_sql_query(match_sql, conn)
conn.close()
assert matched.child_id.is_unique
assert (matched.iloc[:, 2:] > 0).all().all()
matched.to_csv("data/processed/matched.csv", index=False)
Path("sql/match.sql").write_text(match_sql)
print(f"{len(matched)} children matched to {matched.father_id.nunique()} fathers")

text:
What the income relationship looks like
The match produces 170 children and 152 fathers, used in all four regressions:
\[
\log(Y_{\text{child}})=\alpha+\beta\log(Y_{\text{father}})+\varepsilon.
\]
The slope, \(\beta\), is the intergenerational income elasticity (IGE). I average real income before taking logs. Standard errors account for siblings sharing a father. The table reports estimates and 95% confidence limits.

Each dot in Figure 1 places a father’s average family income horizontally and his adult child’s average around 40 vertically. Log scales make equal distances represent equal proportional changes.
The IGE is 0.66: 1% higher parental income is associated with approximately 0.66% higher adult-child income. For a larger comparison, doubling parental income corresponds to roughly 58% higher child income along the fitted relationship. The percentage gap narrows across generations, but a substantial association remains. This does not mean children inherit 66% of their parents’ income.
Look at the spread around the line, though. Children with similar parental incomes often have very different outcomes. The model’s R-squared is 0.18, meaning parental income alone explains about 18% of the variation in logged child income in this sample. That leaves considerable variation unaccounted for. Education, employment, household composition, and measurement error could contribute, but this regression does not separate their roles or establish causes.

In Figure 2, dots show IGE estimates and horizontal lines show 95% confidence intervals. Averaging raises IGE from 0.50 to 0.53 around 30 and 0.57 to 0.66 around 40. All four intervals lie above zero: the positive association survives every definition tested here.
The averaging effect is larger in the later window. Several observations can smooth a temporary job loss or an unusually good year, providing a better picture of usual resources. But I average both generations’ incomes, so this comparison cannot tell us which generation’s temporary fluctuations drive the change.
Age raises a different problem: life-cycle bias. Someone with strong long-term prospects may earn little while still studying, then experience faster income growth. Averaging several early-career years can still miss that later growth. Holding fathers’ average income fixed, IGE rises from 0.53 around 30 to 0.66 around 40. Using the same children rules out changing sample composition as the explanation.
Is that increase precise enough to distinguish from sampling uncertainty? I check directly by relating each child’s change in logged average income to the same parental-income measure. Because the children and predictor stay the same, the slope measures the difference between the two IGEs.

title: Does One Year’s Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Takeaway
My clearest finding is that higher parental family income accompanies higher adult-child family income under every definition I tried. The exact strength is less settled. I would report the later, averaged estimate alongside the alternatives rather than present 0.66 as the definitive answer.
There is another distinction worth keeping in mind: persistence does not tell us whether children are richer than their parents. Incomes could rise across generations while proportional differences associated with family background remain substantial. These regressions do not measure the share of children whose living standards improved.
The sample also shapes the answer. Complete records make comparisons consistent, but leave out people without the required household-head observations or resident-father link. I cannot tell whether including them would raise or lower IGE. This unweighted sample is not nationally representative. Before comparing mobility estimates, I would now ask whose resources they measure, at what ages, and over how many years.

title: Back to Normal—for Which Jobs?
text:
Hello everyone, welcome back!
In my last post, I looked at how income measurement changes our view of economic mobility. This time, I wanted to explore a related issue: how much can an industry total tell us about the jobs within it?
By December 2025, U.S. leisure and hospitality had slightly more jobs than before the pandemic. But were all three major parts of the industry back to their February 2020 job levels?
Accommodation still had about 8% fewer jobs. That gap made me want to look beyond the total.

title: Back to Normal—for Which Jobs?
text:
What the data measure
I use monthly, seasonally adjusted Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll estimates from FRED for January 2019–December 2025. The three components are arts, entertainment, and recreation; accommodation; and food services and drinking places. The dashed line is their total.
Seasonal adjustment removes recurring seasonal patterns. These series count jobs, not people; someone holding two payroll jobs can appear twice. I use the saved October 26, 2026 download because historical estimates can be revised.
For each component, I divide monthly jobs by February 2020 jobs and multiply by 100. An index of 100 means back to baseline; 105 means 5% above it.

from pathlib import Path

Explore the recovery
Start with Recovery index. Hover for job counts and percentage changes, drag the slider to focus on later years, and click legend entries to hide lines. All dates resets the period; Jobs (millions) reveals differences in industry size.

Figure 1. Seasonally adjusted payroll employment, January 2019–December 2025. The dotted line marks February 2020 = 100. Source: BLS via FRED; calculations by the author.
Open the chart separately

title: Back to Normal—for Which Jobs?
text:
After the initial drop
The first thing I notice is how similar the initial losses were. At their spring 2020 lows, all three components had lost roughly half their February jobs. Arts and recreation fell the most, about 52%, but was also the first to regain its old level, in May 2023. That’s what I find interesting here: the biggest initial loss didn’t lead to the longest recovery.
You can check the later years for yourself: move the slider to 2023–2025. By December 2025, arts and recreation was 7.4% above baseline. Food and drink services was just 0.5% above, while accommodation remained 8.0% below.
I wouldn’t describe the first two as equally recovered. Food services first crossed 100 in October 2025 in this download, and by December it was still barely above the line. Arts and recreation had more room to spare. The exact crossing month could shift with revisions; the accommodation shortfall is a much clearer feature of this comparison.

title: Back to Normal—for Which Jobs?
text:
Why the total looks better
Now switch to Jobs (millions). Food and drink services is much larger than the other components: it accounted for about 73% of the industry’s jobs in February 2020. That makes its small net gain important for the total. Setting every series to 100 in February 2020 makes their changes easy to compare, but hides that difference in size.
The job counts help put the recovery together. Arts and recreation added about 184,000 jobs between February 2020 and December 2025. Accommodation had about 169,000 fewer. Those gains and losses almost canceled out. Food services added another 58,000, leaving the published total about 72,000 jobs, or 0.4%, above baseline. The small mismatch in the arithmetic comes from source rounding.
This is why I wanted both views in the same chart. In the index view, accommodation’s slower recovery is easy to see. Switching to job counts shows how increases elsewhere were large enough to cover that gap in the total.

title: Back to Normal—for Which Jobs?
text:
Takeaway
By December 2025, the industry had regained its overall job count, but accommodation hadn’t. So I think a recovery date needs context: it marks when gains elsewhere offset remaining losses, not when every part of the industry recovered.
For me, the useful lesson is to ask where the jobs came back. A gain in arts and recreation can offset a loss in accommodation in a spreadsheet. It doesn’t tell us whether the people who lost accommodation jobs found comparable work, or whether their pay and hours recovered. We’d need different data to answer those questions.
February 2020 is also only a starting point. Matching it doesn’t tell us how many jobs there would have been without the pandemic. So I’d treat crossing 100 as a milestone, then look at which activities are still behind before calling the recovery complete.

title: Why Do the Arrows That Stay on the Same Line Matter So Much?
text:
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors sound intimidating for some people who are not familiar with them. But actually the main idea starts with something simple: an arrow. When a matrix changes an arrow, some arrows stay on the same line. These are eigenvectors, and their eigenvalues describe how they are scaled.
This can be hard to see when we first meet a matrix as a box of numbers. We get busy multiplying entries and lose track of what the calculation does.
But even after I got the picture, one thing still bugged me for a while. For the matrix I’ll use below, these special arrows lie on just two lines, while most arrows turn. And yet, eigenvectors seem to show up everywhere in data science. PCA uses them, Markov chains use them, and even Google’s original PageRank scores come from an eigenvector. Most explanations I’ve seen in textbooks focus on how to calculate those eigenvectors, not on why these few special arrows are such a big deal.
That is the question I want to figure out in my first blog post: if almost every arrow turns, what do the few arrows that don’t turn tell us about all the other ones? This matters when repeated multiplication is used to approximate an eigenvector: knowing the eventual direction does not tell us how many steps are enough. I’ll start with a small example and a picture that may make the idea easier to follow for you. Then we’ll do a little experiment in R and keep applying the same matrix over and over, and see where the turning arrows end up.

title: Why Do the Arrows That Stay on the Same Line Matter So Much?
text:
A small example
Let’s use this matrix as an example:
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Think of a vector as an arrow starting at the origin. The vector \((1,1)\) ends one unit right and one unit up. This R code applies the matrix to that arrow. The symbol %*% means matrix multiplication.

A <- matrix(c(2, 1, 1, 2), nrow = 2)
v <- c(1, 1)
A %*% v

     [,1]
[1,]    3
[2,]    3


The result is \((3,3)\). The arrow becomes three times as long, but still points along the same diagonal. That makes \((1,1)\) an eigenvector of \(A\), with an eigenvalue of 3.
Eigenvectors can also have different lengths. For example, an arrow twice as long along this diagonal still gets stretched by three. Its starting size changes, but its eigenvalue stays the same because the scaling is unchanged.

plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 3.5), ylim = c(0, 3.5),
     xlab = "x", ylab = "y", asp = 1)
arrows(0, 0, 3, 3, col = "red", lwd = 2)
arrows(0, 0, 1, 1, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
text(1, 1, "Before", pos = 2)
text(3, 3, "After", pos = 2)




The blue arrow is the original vector. The red arrow extends three times as far along the same line.




Now try \((1,0)\). This arrow starts out pointing horizontally.

w <- c(1, 0)
A %*% w

     [,1]
[1,]    2
[2,]    1


The result is \((2,1)\), so the arrow tilts upward. It changes direction, which means \((1,0)\) is not an eigenvector of this matrix. The difference is easy to see: one arrow gets longer along its original line, while the other turns.

plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 3.5), ylim = c(0, 3.5),
     xlab = "x", ylab = "y", asp = 1)
arrows(0, 0, 2, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
arrows(0, 0, 1, 0, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
text(1, 0, "Before", pos = 2)
text(2, 1, "After", pos = 2)




The blue arrow (1, 0) is the original vector. The red arrow (2, 1) points in a new direction, so (1, 0) is not an eigenvector.




One detail matters: an arrow is an eigenvector of a particular matrix. A different matrix might turn that same arrow. So the special relationship is between the arrow and the transformation we apply.

title: Why Do the Arrows That Stay on the Same Line Matter So Much?
text:
What the formula means
The definition puts this observation into one equation:
\[
Av = \lambda v, \qquad v \ne 0.
\]
Here, \(v\) is an eigenvector and \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue. For this particular vector, multiplying by the matrix does the same thing as multiplying by one number.
An eigenvalue of one leaves the arrow unchanged. A negative eigenvalue reverses it along the same line. An eigenvalue of zero collapses it to the origin. The zero vector itself is excluded because it has no direction.

title: Why Do the Arrows That Stay on the Same Line Matter So Much?
section: So where do the turning arrows go?
text:
So where do the turning arrows go?
If we keep applying our matrix to \((1,0)\), we get \((2,1)\), then \((5,4)\), then \((14,13)\). The arrow’s length keeps growing, but its direction gets closer to the diagonal through \((1,1)\). How close, and how fast? Let’s track it. The code below applies \(A\) six times and measures the angle between the arrow and the diagonal line through \((1,1)\) after each step.

# Angle, in degrees, between an arrow and the diagonal line through (1, 1)
angle_to_diagonal <- function(v) {
  # size of the part along (1, 1)
  along  <- abs(v[1] + v[2]) / sqrt(2)
  # size of the part along (1, -1)
  across <- abs(v[1] - v[2]) / sqrt(2)
  atan2(across, along) * 180 / pi
}

v <- c(1, 0)
trajectory <- data.frame()
for (step in 0:6) {
  trajectory <- rbind(trajectory,
                      data.frame(step = step, x = v[1], y = v[2],
                                 angle = angle_to_diagonal(v)))
  v <- as.vector(A %*% v)
}

             col.names = c("Step", "x", "y", "Angle to diagonal (degrees)"))

The angle starts at 45 degrees and drops below a tenth of a degree after just six steps. And if you look at the numbers closely, there’s a pattern. As the angle gets smaller, it falls to roughly a third of its previous value: 6.34, 2.12, 0.71. Why a third?
That happens because the part along the eigenvector \((1,1)\) grows faster than the other part. Here’s what I mean: we can split any arrow into two pieces: one piece along \((1,1)\) and one piece along the other eigenvector of \(A\), which is \((1,-1)\). For example, \((1,0)\) is just half of \((1,1)\) plus half of \((1,-1)\). Every time we apply \(A\), the \((1,1)\) piece gets multiplied by its eigenvalue, 3, and the \((1,-1)\) piece gets multiplied by its eigenvalue, 1, so it doesn’t change at all. After \(k\) steps we get
\[
A^k \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{pmatrix} = \frac{3^k}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Every step, the \((1,1)\) piece gets three times bigger compared to the other piece, so the arrow leans more and more toward the diagonal. That’s where the three comes from. It’s just the ratio of the two eigenvalues, 3 divided by 1.
At this point I wondered if \((1,0)\) was just a lucky choice. To check, I tried sixteen arrows pointing in all different directions. I applied \(A\) to each of them five times, and then shrank every arrow back to length one so we only compare directions.

directions <- seq(0, 337.5, by = 22.5) * pi / 180
# one arrow per column
before <- rbind(cos(directions), sin(directions))

after <- before
for (step in 1:5) after <- A %*% after
# rescale to length one
after <- sweep(after, 2, sqrt(colSums(after^2)), "/")

# the two arrows that start exactly along the other eigenvector, (1, -1)
on_other_line <- abs(before[1, ] + before[2, ]) < 1e-8
arrow_col <- ifelse(on_other_line, "#CD6600", "blue")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
panels <- list(before, after)
titles <- c("Before", "After applying A five times")
for (i in 1:2) {
  plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(-1.1, 1.1), ylim = c(-1.1, 1.1),
       xlab = "x", ylab = "y", asp = 1, main = titles[i])
  abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
  arrows(0, 0, panels[[i]][1, ], panels[[i]][2, ],
         col = arrow_col, lwd = 2, length = 0.08)
}




Left: sixteen arrows before applying A. Right: the same arrows after applying A five times, rescaled to length one. The blue arrows are now close to the dashed diagonal line. The two orange arrows start on the line through (1, -1) and stay there.




It wasn’t luck. After five steps, fourteen of the sixteen arrows are close to the diagonal line. Some point toward \((1,1)\) and some toward \((-1,-1)\), but it’s the same line. The only two that don’t are the orange ones. An arrow starting exactly along the other eigenvector, \((1,-1)\), would stay unchanged instead, because its eigenvalue is 1. These two remain exceptions because they start exactly on that line. If you push one of them even a tiny bit off of it, that tiny piece along \((1,1)\) gets tripled every step, and eventually it takes over too.

title: Why Do the Arrows That Stay on the Same Line Matter So Much?
section: Does it matter how far apart the eigenvalues are?
text:
Does it matter how far apart the eigenvalues are?
If the three really comes from dividing the two eigenvalues, then the speed should change when the eigenvalues get closer together. I wanted to check this, so I made a second matrix, \(B\). It has the same eigenvectors as \(A\), and its biggest eigenvalue is still 3. The only difference is that its other eigenvalue is 2.7 instead of 1:
\[
B = \begin{pmatrix}2.85 & 0.15 \\ 0.15 & 2.85\end{pmatrix}.
\]

B <- matrix(c(2.85, 0.15, 0.15, 2.85), nrow = 2)
eigen(A)$values

[1] 3 1

eigen(B)$values

[1] 3.0 2.7


R confirms it: \(A\) has eigenvalues 3 and 1, and \(B\) has 3 and 2.7. Now let’s start both matrices from \((1,0)\), apply each one 40 times, and watch the angle.

track_angle <- function(M, v, n_steps) {
  angles <- numeric(n_steps + 1)
  for (k in 0:n_steps) {
    angles[k + 1] <- angle_to_diagonal(v)
    v <- as.vector(M %*% v)
  }
  angles
}

steps <- 0:40
angle_A <- track_angle(A, c(1, 0), 40)
angle_B <- track_angle(B, c(1, 0), 40)

# First step at which the arrow is within one degree of the diagonal
c(A = min(steps[angle_A < 1]), B = min(steps[angle_B < 1]))

 A  B 
 4 39 



plot(steps, angle_B, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 45),
     xlab = "Number of times the matrix is applied",
     ylab = "Angle to diagonal (degrees)")
lines(steps, angle_A, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
text(2.3, 7.5, "A", pos = 4)
text(12, 19, "B", pos = 4)
legend("topright", legend = c("A: eigenvalues 3 and 1", "B: eigenvalues 3 and 2.7"),
       col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")




How far the arrow is from the diagonal after each step, starting from (1, 0). The dashed line marks one degree. A gets there after 4 steps, while B needs 39.




This was the part that surprised me the most. Both matrices stretch \((1,1)\) by exactly 3, so if you only looked at the biggest eigenvalue, you would think they behave the same. They don’t. With \(A\), the arrow is within one degree of the diagonal after 4 steps. With \(B\), it takes 39 steps, almost ten times as many. Both counts use the same starting arrow and the same one-degree cutoff. The reason is the same as before: each step, the \((1,1)\) piece gains on the other piece by the ratio of the eigenvalues. For \(A\) that ratio is \(3/1 = 3\), but for \(B\) it is only \(3/2.7 \approx 1.11\). That’s why, with \(B\), the arrow keeps “remembering” where it started for so long.

title: Why Do the Arrows That Stay on the Same Line Matter So Much?
text:
What I learned from this
Eigenvectors show us special directions within a transformation. Eigenvalues tell us what happens along those directions. That definition felt pretty abstract to me until I actually ran these experiments. Two things finally clicked.
The first is that eigenvectors are not just weird exceptions. I used to think of them as the few arrows that happen not to turn. For our matrix, repeated multiplication brings any arrow with a nonzero piece along \((1,1)\) closer to that line. So the eigenvector tells us where those turning arrows are heading. This helps me understand why eigenvectors matter in applications such as PageRank, where repeated multiplication is used to find a steady-state distribution.
The second is that computing the eigenvalues isn’t enough. We should also compare them. For a fixed starting arrow, the ratio of the smaller eigenvalue to the larger one tells us how quickly the other component loses ground. With 3 and 1 it took 4 steps; with 3 and 2.7 it took 39. For me, this means that running both calculations for the same number of steps would not give equally accurate directions. I need to check how close the result actually is, rather than assume that a few more steps will be enough.
One thing we need to be careful about, though: the standard power-method argument assumes one eigenvalue is strictly larger in absolute value than the others and the starting arrow has a nonzero component in its direction. For example, a matrix that rotates every arrow by 90 degrees has no real eigenvectors at all, so the arrows just keep spinning around and never settle on any line.
So, back to my question. The few arrows that don’t turn matter because they help explain where the other arrows in our experiment tend to point, and the eigenvalue ratio tells us how quickly they approach that line. For me, that’s a much more useful way to think about eigenvectors than just remembering \(Av = \lambda v\).

Eric Darve, The Power Method.
Christopher D. Manning, Prabhakar Raghavan, and Hinrich Schütze, The PageRank Computation, Introduction to Information Retrieval.
